newsitem.title: USA: Police, separatists far apart in Texas.
newsitem.headline: Police, separatists far apart in Texas.

text.p: Police on Tuesday indicated that a three-day standoff with armed Texas separatists holed up in a mountain compound would soon end peacefully, but the leader of the dissident group gave a sharply conflicting view and said there was a "state of war."

Texas Department of Public Safety spokesman Mike Cox told reporters that negotiations to end the siege with the Republic of Texas group, which advocates the secession of Texas from the United States, were at "a sensitive stage but progressing well."
He warned that "we are dealing with some very complex issues which take time to resolve," but said communication with the separatists was "frequent, positive and open."

But Richard McLaren, self-styled "ambassador" for the Republic of Texas, said peace would not come easily. He has told police negotiators that he and his followers were prepared to die defending their erstwhile republic.

"We're not going to be pulled out like the Freemen. Those boys, if you notice, haven't got a trial yet ... so, we're not going to get screwed and tattooed like everyone else," McLaren told KHOU-TV in Houston.
The Freemen were an anti-government militia group in Montana who had a protracted standoff with police before surrendering last year.
McLaren, a 43-year-old organic vintner from Missouri, said his dream of an independent Texas was already a reality because he had filed papers declaring the republic with the United Nations.
"This is our country, last week the last U.N. filing was done. We are under self-governance. We're in a state of war," he said.

The standoff began on Sunday when Republic members grabbed two hostages from a nearby home in retaliation for the arrest of their security chief, Robert Scheidt, on charges he had illegal weapons. One of the hostages was injured when the Republic members shot their way into his house.

The hostages were released on Monday in a swap for Scheidt, but criminal charges including aggravated kidnapping were filed against six of the 13 Republic members said to be in the tin-walled compound. The charges carry penalties of up to 99 years in prison.

About 120 heavily armed police officers have flooded into the rugged Davis Mountains in west Texas where they are poised to move in to arrest the group by force if they do not surrender. The police arsenal includes two 13-ton armoured personnel carriers -- called "Bubba 1" and "Bubba 2" -- lent by an east Texas sheriff.

The Republic of Texas group was formed in late 1995 and claims to have thousands of members and ties to anti-government militias. It wants Texas to secede from the United States and become an independent nation, as it was for nine years after breaking away from Mexico in 1836.

McLaren was charged with contempt in December for failing to appear in federal court on charges related to bogus liens issued by the Republic. Since then he and several followers have holed up inside the compound, which is about 200 miles (320 km) southeast of El Paso, Texas.
Police, fearful of touching off the anger of militia groups, have not attempted to arrest him for the earlier charge, but Texas Attorney General Dan Morales said on Tuesday the situation had changed.

"Members of this group are no longer novelties or curiosities, they now are bona fide criminals. What is occurring in west Texas is terrorism, pure and simple," he told a news conference in Austin, Texas.
McLaren said the Republic of Texas, armed with its own indictments and arrest warrants, would arrest Morales and other state officials.
"I've got indictments on that son of a bitch, and there's warrants on him and all of them, and there's boys in east Texas and north Texas looking for him right now," he said.
